newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's money market - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's money market - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

In the course of exorcising apprehensions about the abolition of exchange controls, one of our eminent economic philosophers -- no name, no pack drill -- has recently opined that with the purchase of foreign currency deposits by South African residents there is a corresponding acquisition of rand currency deposits by non-residents.

This being so, money or capital cannot possibly leave the country; there is simply a swap of ownership and the only change is a possible rand exchange rate movement. It is accordingly a myth to refer to capital flight.
One is inclined to use a term related to bovine scatology, but better to adopt his own aggressive style and say: Wrong!

In the real world a South African wishing to invest abroad or remit capital, if that may be presumed for the moment to be free of any exchange control restriction, does so through the intermediary of a bank.
For example, the domestic claim of the South African resident on the South African bank, say of nine million rand, is transformed into a claim of $2 million on a New York bank.

But in the process the claims of the South African bank on the New York bank will be reduced by $2 million. A reverse process will happen with an American bank's balances in New York and a domestic rand claim arising in favour of the American.

But further to these transactions the South African bank could normalise its New York working balance by either buying U.S. dollars from the Reserve Bank or selling them to it. In the case of restoring the bank's balances there will have been a shift of balances in New York from the Reserve Bank to the SOuth African bank, and a reduction in the domestic claims of the South African bank on the Reserve Bank which, in turn, will probably require restoring to the minimum statutory level through bank accommodation -- and vice versa.

The essence of the matter is that capital can leave the country and, in the process, affect the foreign reserves of the Reserve Bank as reflected in its position on New York, and also the money market shortage as reflected in the extent of accommodation received from the Reserve Bank.

Capital coming into the country will increase the reserves and reduce the money market shortage. The mechanisms involve a shift of balances through the banking system and its international correspondents, and not a swap of claims on the South African domestic banks between residents and non-residents.

A current concern of the Reserve Bank must be the asymmetry of a tentativeness of non-residents about investing in South Africa and the appetite of South Africans, generally, to get money out of the country and of South African institutions wishing to diversify their portfolios by investing abroad. In a situation of a current account deficit running at an annual rate of 12 billion rand to 13 billion rand and foreign reserves of less than a month and a half of import cover there is understandable reluctance on the part of the Reserve Bank to move with further relaxation of exchange controls, which is confined in large measure to residents.

One suspects also that the Bank fears that it would not be politic to do so. A legitimised haemorrhaging of institutional funds abroad would, indeed, be unjustifiable in a situation of low domestic savings and a massive need for infrastructural development. The institutions' dilemma is that the scope for further investment in shopping malls and office blocks is limited but there is an ongoing responsibility to policy holders.
However, to return to the matter of the money market shortage which, as argued, is clearly affected by the overall balance of payments situation:

The money market shortage is also fundamentally affected by the state of the central government's account, or Exchequer account, held with the Reserve Bank. The Exchequer account balance rises as taxes or loans proceeds flow from the private sector through the intermediary of the commercial banks, involving a drain on the reserve balances held with the Reserve Bank that need to be restored through bank accommodation - and vice versa.

This ebb and flow of funds between government and the private sector can be considerable and unnecessarily disruptive. As originally recommended by the de Kock Commission, special Loan and Tax accounts of government have been established with the commercial banks. These accounts can accommodate the bulk of the transfers between the private sector and the government without affecting the money market shortage. On the other hand they can be an instrument for influencing the money market shortage by shifting funds between them and the Exchequer account. But the process is limited by the availability of funds in the respective accounts.

Developments in 1996 have subjected the money market shortage to considerable pressure. As the Governor said in his address, the shortage increased from 5.1 billion rand at the end of December 1996 to 11.0 billion rand at the end of April, after which it receded to 8.6 billion rand at the end of July.

The primary cause of the leap in the shortage at the end of April was, of course, the reversal of short-term capital flows in the balance of payments, negating long-term capital inflows and exposing the deficit on current account. The Reserve Bank's foreign exchange reserves had to bear the brunt of the overall deficit on the balance of payments.

But during April when the full force of the currency crisis hit the country the Bank was caught napping in that it allowed the Exchequer balance to rise from a mere nine million rand to 2.8 billion rand, so exacerbating the impact of the balance of payments on the market shortage. However, it reversed this position in May and June when the Exchequer balances dropped to 270 million rand and 315 million rand, respectively. Meanwhile the Tax and Loan account balances have fluctuated between 7.4 billion rand and 5.4 billion rand. The Reserve Bank allowed the Exchequer balance to creep up to 848 million rand at the end of July.

In sum the money market shortage is primarily affected by the balance of payments situation, but can be moderated or accentuated by management of government's balances. The overall balance of payments situation is essentially beyond the control or influence of the Reserve Bank although, theoretically, the interest rate weapon will have a corrective medium-term effect. But the Bank's freedom to change interest rates through the Bank rate is limited by other domestic considerations.

Pressure on the money market shortage will be manifested in pressure on money market rates to rise -- without collusion on the part of the banks. This can and has put the Reserve Bank between a rock and a hard place for it is limited in its power to control the money market shortage and it may be inopportune to accede to pressures to raise the Bank rate. The ultimate way out of the dilemma could be for the Bank to relax the reserve requireents, but again it is inhibited by considerations of promoting credit creation and even of losing control of the Bank rate mechanism.
One is reminded of the Gilbert & Sullivan couplet:
When constabulatory duty's to be done, to be done
The policeman's lot is not a happy one, happy one!
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
